content: For moderate-to-severe depression, combine antidepressant pharmacotherapy with structured psychological treatment. First-line pharmacotherapy: SSRIs (fluoxetine 20–60 mg, sertraline 50–200 mg, escitalopram 10–20 mg). Ensure adequate trial: 4–6 weeks at therapeutic dose before switching. Psychological treatment: CBT, interpersonal therapy (IPT), or behavioural activation — minimum 12 sessions. Assess and document suicidal ideation at every visit using a validated scale (PHQ-9, C-SSRS). Safety planning is mandatory when PHQ-9 item 9 ≥ 1 or any ideation disclosed.

source: APA Practice Guideline for MDD (3rd Edition)
content: Treatment-resistant depression (TRD) is defined as failure to achieve remission after two adequate antidepressant trials of different classes. Augmentation strategies: lithium (serum level 0.6–1.0 mEq/L), atypical antipsychotics (aripiprazole 2–15 mg, quetiapine 50–300 mg, brexpiprazole 1–3 mg), thyroid hormone (T3, 25–50 mcg). For TRD with acute suicidality or psychosis: esketamine (Spravato) 56–84 mg intranasal, supervised in certified healthcare setting. ECT indicated for severe, life-threatening TRD, or when rapid response is needed.

Screen all perinatal patients at first prenatal visit, second or third trimester visit, and 4–6 weeks postpartum using Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). Score ≥10 warrants further assessment; ≥13 indicates probable depression. SSRI use in pregnancy: benefits generally outweigh risks for moderate-to-severe depression. Sertraline and escitalopram have most safety data in pregnancy. Brexanolone (Zulresso) IV is FDA-approved specifically for postpartum depression — 60-hour infusion in certified setting. Breastfeeding compatible SSRIs: sertraline, paroxetine (lowest milk levels).

GAD first-line treatment: SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram, paroxetine) or SNRIs (venlafaxine XR 75–225 mg, duloxetine 60–120 mg). Buspirone 15–60 mg/day is an effective non-habit-forming option for chronic GAD, particularly in elderly patients. Benzodiazepines: reserve for acute anxiety exacerbations, short-term only (2–4 weeks). Avoid long-term benzodiazepine use — associated with dependence, cognitive impairment, and increased fall risk in elderly. Psychological treatment: CBT is gold standard (12–16 sessions). Relaxation training and mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) are evidence-based adjuncts.

Panic Disorder first-line: SSRIs (paroxetine, sertraline, fluoxetine) or venlafaxine XR. Start low and titrate slowly — patients with panic are sensitive to initial activating side effects. CBT with interoceptive exposure and panic control treatment (PCT): highly effective, 12 sessions. Avoid alprazolam for long-term management due to high dependence potential. Clonazepam 0.5–2 mg BID may bridge acute phase if CBT not immediately available. Agoraphobia: requires graduated exposure therapy — do not allow avoidance to consolidate.

First-line psychotherapy for PTSD: Prolonged Exposure (PE), Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT), and EMDR — all strongly recommended. Individual trauma-focused CBT preferred over group therapy. First-line pharmacotherapy: sertraline 50–200 mg or paroxetine 20–60 mg (FDA-approved). Prazosin 1–15 mg at bedtime for trauma-related nightmares. Avoid benzodiazepines — associated with worse PTSD outcomes and impair extinction learning during trauma-focused therapy. Assess for comorbid MDD, substance use, and TBI. Dissociative subtype (present in ~15–30%): may need modified PE protocol with stabilization phase first.

source: NICE Guideline NG62 — Borderline Personality Disorder
content: BPD first-line treatment: structured psychological therapy — DBT (Dialectical Behaviour Therapy) is the most evidence-based intervention. DBT consists of individual therapy + skills group (mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness). MBT (Mentalization-Based Treatment) and Schema Therapy are second-line evidence-based options. Pharmacotherapy: no medication is FDA-approved for BPD as primary treatment. Target symptom clusters: mood lability (mood stabilizers — lamotrigine, valproate), impulsivity/aggression (low-dose atypicals), transient psychosis (low-dose antipsychotics). Avoid polypharmacy. Crisis plan must be documented — includes self-harm safety protocols and hospital contact numbers.

Acute mania treatment: lithium (serum level 0.8–1.2 mEq/L), valproate (serum level 50–125 mcg/mL), or atypical antipsychotics (olanzapine, risperidone, aripiprazole, quetiapine). Antidepressant monotherapy is contraindicated in Bipolar I — risk of precipitating manic switch. Maintenance: lithium remains gold standard for relapse prevention (also reduces suicide risk). Lamotrigine 200–400 mg/day effective for bipolar depression prevention; slow titration mandatory (25 mg/week) to reduce Stevens-Johnson syndrome risk. Quetiapine and lurasidone are FDA-approved for bipolar depression. Monitor: lithium levels, renal function, TFTs every 6 months. Thyroid and renal toxicity risk with long-term use.

First-episode psychosis (FEP): use the lowest effective dose of an SGA (second-generation antipsychotic). Recommended agents: aripiprazole, risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine. FEP typically requires lower doses. Clozapine: reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failure of ≥2 antipsychotics). Requires ANC monitoring (neutrophil count): baseline, weekly × 6 months, biweekly × 6 months, then monthly. Long-acting injectables (LAI): consider for adherence issues — paliperidone palmitate, aripiprazole lauroxil, risperidone microspheres. Target: positive symptoms, negative symptoms, social functioning. Coordinated Specialty Care (CSC) for FEP: evidence-based multimodal team approach.

Adult ADHD first-line pharmacotherapy: stimulants — methylphenidate (IR/ER, 5–60 mg/day) or amphetamine salts (10–60 mg/day). OROS methylphenidate (Concerta), mixed amphetamine salts XR (Adderall XR) have evidence for adults. Non-stimulant alternatives: atomoxetine 80–100 mg/day (FDA-approved, preferred when substance use disorder co-occurs), viloxazine 200–400 mg/day, bupropion (off-label). Monitor: BP, HR, weight, appetite, sleep, and potential for misuse. CBT for ADHD adults: improves organization, time management, emotional dysregulation. Assess for comorbid anxiety, depression, and substance use — extremely common in adult ADHD.
